note: Levels: info (advice), caution (possible risk of error), serious (the model may not be estimable), limit (case not covered by the app). Fields computed by the engine: epv = events / params; spp = n / params.

warnings.text: Fewer than 10 events per parameter. The rule of 10 is conservative and estimates are often acceptable with 5-9 events; you may want to reduce the number of parameters and run sensitivity analyses.

Fewer than 5 events per parameter: the estimates may be biased. Options to consider: fewer covariates chosen with a DAG, Firth's correction, or a propensity score, which summarises the confounders in a single parameter.
Fewer than 2 subjects per parameter: simulation studies suggest that even linear regression may not estimate the coefficients well.
For a prediction model, consider calculating the minimum sample size with Riley's criteria (the pmsampsize package): events per variable alone are usually not enough.
Few events per parameter for a prediction model. LASSO and ridge may not solve the problem: in small samples their effect can be unstable.

Random forests, SVMs and neural networks may need more than 10 times the events per variable of logistic regression. In the studies reviewed, at low risk of bias, they did not predict better than logistic regression on average.

Consider assessing discrimination (AUC or C statistic), calibration and clinical utility (decision curve). Internal validation with bootstrapping or cross-validation is generally recommended over apparent performance alone.
The coefficients of a prediction model are generally not interpretable as causal effects.

Stepwise selection based on p-values is generally discouraged. For a causal effect, a DAG can guide the choice of covariates; for prediction, prior knowledge or penalisation with an adequate sample size.

Observational study: the literature recommends stating the causal aim, choosing the confounders with a DAG and reporting mainly the effect of the exposure rather than the coefficients of the covariates.
When comparing treatments with observational data, specifying the target trial (eligibility criteria, time zero, treatment strategies) can help avoid immortal time bias.
In an RCT, adjusting for pre-specified prognostic factors usually increases power. Defining the estimand (ICH E9(R1)) is also advisable, especially for intercurrent events.
A case-control study can only estimate the odds ratio: absolute risks and risk ratios need external data on incidence.

With a common outcome the odds ratio tends to exaggerate the risk ratio. Consider estimating the risk ratio with modified Poisson regression, or showing predicted probabilities alongside the odds ratio.
Choosing the model on a proportional hazards test alone is discouraged. Consider looking at the curves and, if the hazard ratio changes over time, reporting hazard ratios by period or the RMST.
With competing events, one minus Kaplan-Meier tends to overestimate the risk: the cumulative incidence, with results for all causes, is usually preferable.
Dichotomising a continuous exposure is generally discouraged: it loses power and can introduce bias. For non-linear relationships, splines or fractional polynomials are an option.
Classifying an exposure that changes over time at baseline can create immortal time bias. Time-dependent covariates or target trial emulation are options to consider.
Little missing data: a complete-case analysis is often acceptable, but it is good practice to report how much is missing and in which variables.
Non-negligible missing data: consider describing the amount and the pattern, multiple imputation if missingness can be explained by observed variables (MAR), and sensitivity analyses.
Estimates with confidence intervals are generally more informative than p-values alone. The p-value does not measure the size of an effect, nor the probability that the hypothesis is true.
If you assess an interaction, it is recommended to report the effect in each stratum, on both the additive and the multiplicative scale.

For a descriptive question, adjusting for confounders is usually not needed and can change the quantity being described. It is generally preferable to stratify by, or standardise over, variables chosen in advance.
Consider stating the target population (person, place and time), the outcome and the measure of occurrence (for example prevalence on a date, incidence, mean time to event) before the analysis.
In a cross-over trial, carry-over effects can bias the comparison; an adequate wash-out period and an analysis by sequence group are usually recommended.
Time-to-event outcomes rarely suit a cross-over design: the event can end the follow-up before the second period.

For non-inferiority or equivalence, the margin needs to be pre-specified and justified, and the conclusion comes from comparing the confidence interval with the margin. Analysing both the intention-to-treat and the per-protocol populations is recommended.
With fewer than 5 studies, especially of very different sizes, the between-study variance is estimated poorly and even the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman method needs extra caution.
The pooled estimate is an average effect: the prediction interval shows how much the effect may vary between settings and is usually more informative for practice.
In a Bayesian analysis it is recommended to justify the prior distributions, to run sensitivity analyses with different priors, and to report the posterior distribution with credible intervals.
With few events, a Bayesian analysis with weakly informative priors is one option that can stabilise the estimates; priors expressed as prior data make their weight visible.

If confounders change over time and may be affected by earlier exposure, standard regression adjustment can be biased: g-methods (marginal structural models, g-formula) are designed for this situation.

With patients starting either drug for the first time, a new-user (incident user) active-comparator design is usually recommended: follow-up starts at initiation and covariates are measured before it, which avoids prevalent-user bias.
Including prevalent users without aligning time zero can introduce bias: they are 'survivors' of the early period of treatment, and their covariates may already be affected by the drug.
